title: Writing Workshop
description: Writing is key to success in graduate school and in many careers in science, but there are aspects of it that people can struggle with (e.g., clearly communicating complex ideas, writing regularly, writing for general audiences, etc.). In this course, students will (i) learn about and discuss the mechanics of writing academic papers, (ii) receive feedback on their writing and learn to provide constructive feedback to others, and (iii) engage in reading and discussion about time management, handling rejection, and other challenges that academic writers may face.
prerequisites_raw: Graduate standing in PBS or DYNS

title: Controversies and Debates in Evolution and Human Behavior
description: Controversies abound in evolutionary approaches to human behavior, concerning both basic theoretical issues (e.g., modularity and domain specificity) and broader societal issues (e.g., the relationship between evolutionary theory, racism, and sexism). In this class, students engage with some of the most fundamental debates in evolutionary behavioral sciences, interrogating evidence and assumptions concerning our theoretical positions and responsibilities as scientists.

title: Adaptionist Modeling
description: Natural selection creates machines that are improbably good at solving reproductive problems. Knowledge of the problems recurrently faced by human ancestors can therefore give psychologists useful clues as to the likely design features of the mind. But how exactly does one do this psychological reverse engineering? That is, given a problem, how can one go about identifying what a good solution would look like? Topics will include basic decision theory, evolutionary game theory, signaling theory, reinforcement learning, Bayesian reasoning, and other approaches. Students will learn the basic logic of these approaches, discuss applications to psychology, and use these approaches to generate novel hypotheses.

title: Social Change
description: Focuses on generating discussion of and testable research ideas based on the last 20 years of literature in the social psychology of social change. Students select topics of interest to them or choose from suggested topics, provide a brief overview of key work on the topic or approach, and propose research ideas for discussion and feedback.

title: Hormones and Cognition
description: The brain is part of a larger, integrated biological system. One example of this whole-brain, whole-body level of integration is the interaction between hormone-producing organs in the body (e.g. gonads) and the nervous system. For example, estrogen receptors are found throughout the entire brain, which hints at the powerful role this hormone plays in shaping the brain and, ultimately, behavior. This course introduces students to the impact hormones have on brain structure, function and cognition. Through close examination of primary source material, review articles, book chapters and popular media, we consider hormones role in shaping brain function with a life-course perspective.

title: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on Emotion and Decision-Making.
description: This graduate seminar explores how scholars study emotion and decision-making, drawing on insights from philosophy, psychology, neuroscience, and computational methods. Students will critically engage with theories and methods across disciplines to examine the foundations of emotion and decision-making.
